purpose: Prevents attackers from compromising authentication mechanisms to impersonate legitimate users through stolen tokens, credential stuffing, or weak authentication implementation.
summary: Broken Authentication occurs when authentication mechanisms are implemented incorrectly, allowing attackers to compromise authentication tokens or exploit implementation flaws to assume other users' identities, whether temporarily or permanently.
expectedStatementElements: What authentication mechanism is used (API keys, OAuth, JWT) and how tokens are issued, validated, and expired
What protections exist against credential stuffing and brute-force attacks (rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA)
How authentication tokens are protected from theft or leakage (in transit, in logs, in URLs)
Whether weak or default credentials, or unauthenticated endpoints that should require authentication, have been identified and remediated
evidenceExamples: Authentication architecture documentation (token type, issuance, expiration, revocation)
Rate limiting or account lockout configuration for authentication endpoints
Security scan results checking for tokens exposed in logs, URLs, or error messages
Inventory of endpoints confirming authentication is required where expected
commonGaps: No rate limiting or lockout exists on authentication endpoints, enabling credential stuffing
Tokens don't expire, or expiration is set unreasonably long
Tokens or credentials appear in URLs, logs, or error messages where they can leak
Some endpoints that should require authentication are unintentionally left open
interviewQuestions: What stops an attacker from brute-forcing or credential-stuffing your login endpoint?
How long do authentication tokens live, and can they be revoked?
Could a token or credential ever end up in a log file, URL, or error message?
How do you verify that every endpoint requiring authentication actually enforces it?
